name: Uniform deployment on a ring

origin.note: Self-deployment of mobile sensors on a ring (ALGOSENSORS 2006).

related.relation: Both spread robots out; scattering only needs distinct positions, deployment needs equal spacing.

summary: Robots on a circle must spread out to equal spacing.
statement: $n$ robots on a circle (or a ring of length $L$) must reach positions at equal distance $d=L/n$ from their neighbours and stop. Spreading on a segment is the one-dimensional analogue.

primer.intro: Picture $n$ guards spread at random along a circular wall who must spread out so that every two neighbours are the same distance apart. In uniform deployment, $n$ robots sit at distinct points of a circle of length $L$ and must reach positions where every gap between consecutive robots is exactly $d = L/n$, and then stop. In the basic version robots are oblivious (they forget everything after each move), asynchronous (an adversary decides when each robot looks and moves, and a robot may see others in mid-move), and agree on which way is clockwise (an *oriented* ring).

ideas.title: Close the gap in front of you, only clockwise
ideas.idea:
Robots know $d$. Each time a robot is activated:
1. Look clockwise and measure the distance to the next robot.
2. If that distance is at most $d$, do nothing.
3. If it is more than $d$, move clockwise until you are exactly $d$ behind that robot.
ideas.analysis: All gaps add up to $L = nd$, so if some gap is smaller than $d$, another is larger. Robots only move clockwise, so the robot in front never comes closer; a robot whose gap is at least $d$ therefore never again has a gap below $d$, and the number of such robots never decreases. [Flocchini2008Deployment] prove that this protocol (Uniform Known) reaches exact deployment in finite time, even with limited visibility $2d$; when $d$ is unknown, a "go to the half" rule reaches every gap within any $\varepsilon$ of $d$. No running-time bound is recorded in the catalogue.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that a shared sense of direction plus one number ($d$) turns an impossible task into a three-line rule.

ideas.title: Two mirror-image teams that always overshoot
ideas.idea:
Without a shared clockwise direction exact deployment is impossible, even with full memory and SSYNC activation. Take $n = 4$: black robots at two opposite points, white robots at two opposite points, the white pair rotated by a small angle from the uniform position. Black robots think clockwise is one way, white robots think it is the other, so each black robot sees exactly what each white robot sees, in mirror image. The adversary then plays:
1. If moving only the blacks would not finish the job, move only the blacks (the picture keeps the same two-team shape).
2. If moving only the blacks would finish, then by the mirror image moving only the whites would also finish; so move both. Each team closes the same gap, together they overshoot, and again the picture has the same shape.
3. Alternate between starting with the blacks and the whites, so every robot moves infinitely often.
ideas.analysis: Every round leaves the robots in two rotated half-teams, never equally spaced, so the algorithm never finishes [Flocchini2008Deployment]. The argument works for every even $n$ with two interleaved regular $n/2$-gons. It is why the catalogued variant assumes an oriented ring.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is a model example of an adversary that exploits mirror symmetry and the freedom to choose who moves.

history: Self-deployment asked **under which assumptions robots can spread uniformly** around a ring [Flocchini2008Deployment] or along a segment [Cohen2008Spreading]: orientation and knowledge of the target distance turned out to be the deciding factors.

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or epochs (ASYNC) until the task is done; "finite" when only solvability is known

measures.name: Colours
measures.description: colours of the light per robot (0 for oblivious robots)

variants.title: Oriented ring, asynchronous, oblivious
variants.summary: On an oriented ring oblivious asynchronous robots deploy exactly if they know $d$, and within any $\varepsilon$ if they do not.

preconditions: exact deployment without orientation, even semi-synchronous

results.note: Introductory and current best; $\varepsilon$-approximate deployment without knowing $d$.

open: Is knowledge of $d$ necessary for exact deployment on an oriented ring? Which capabilities allow asynchronous exact deployment on unoriented rings? [Flocchini2008Deployment]
variants.notes: The chirality value stands for an oriented ring. Spreading on a segment: [Cohen2008Spreading].

figure.caption: Uniform deployment on a ring: robots on a circle of length $L$ must reach positions at distance exactly $d = L/n$ from their neighbours and stop [Flocchini2008Deployment]. The animation runs their rule for an oriented ring with known $d$: an activated robot whose clockwise gap (red) exceeds $d$ moves clockwise along the ring until it is exactly $d$ behind the next robot; here the asynchronous adversary activates one robot at a time.
